issues.issue: "The Contract shall be the present contract with the changes made by this Memorandum" leaves the identity of "the present contract" (the 1981-84 booklet plus side letters?) to be worked out. The reach is narrow but a court could be asked what documents make up "the Contract".

"This amount" has no certain referent — it may mean only the $43.35 increase, or the whole journeyman scale as increased. The clause also does not say at what rate or to which fund contributions are "made on" it.

The direction to make pension and welfare contributions appears only for the 1987 increase and is absent from the 1988-1992 increases in paragraph 2(b) and from the 13-H.1 percentage revision, leaving whether contributions follow the later increases contestable.

The passive "shall be contributed" does not say who bears the $3.67 — it is described as coming "from wages and after taxes", which reads as an employee deduction, yet it is styled a contribution to the Welfare Fund. "Per shift ... (maximum of five (5) shifts)" also leaves the measuring period unstated.

The same $3.67 figure is inserted into Section 13-H.1 by the Appendix revision as "an after tax deduction from wages of $3.67" after "per shift", so the two texts may describe one obligation or two cumulative ones.

"Payments retroactive to March 31, 1987" does not say whether it covers only wages or also the pension, welfare and $3.67 contributions referred to in the same subparagraph. The scope of the retroactive obligation is therefore open.
The sentence is truncated mid-phrase ("increased by $35 a if"), so the unit of the increase is missing from the text as written.

Paragraph 2(a) directs that "[p]ension and welfare contributions shall be made on this amount" for the 1987 increase, while this subparagraph sets four further increases without any such direction, inviting an expressio unius argument about contributions on the later raises.

The COLA mechanism is left entirely to "the relevant provisions of the Contract", which are not identified and are themselves being amended by this Memorandum. Which formula governs is therefore not fixed by the text.

The index sentence is enclosed in brackets, so whether it is an operative term or an editorial note is uncertain, and it says only that the Index "shall be used for measurement of the change" without a base period or formula.

Words are plainly missing between "at the Edison, New Jersey" and "by The Times within the Northeast Corridor", so the geographic scope of the Contract's application — Edison only, or every facility operated in the Corridor — cannot be read off the text.
"Committed to the orderly, successful and efficient start-up and operation" states an aspiration with no measurable content, and whether it creates any enforceable duty is open.
This recital-style commitment sits against the operative arbitration and layoff-protection sentences that follow in paragraph 3, and could be urged as colouring or enlarging them.

The layoff protection is limited to layoffs "because of the introduction of automated processes", while the sentence otherwise addresses "innovations in methods of operation" generally, so the protected class of layoffs is narrower than the subject matter and the causal test is unstated.

The sentence is incomplete ("on the date of the commencement of built facility"), so the second listing date cannot be identified, and "all such protected regular situation holders" depends on the preceding sentence's uncertain scope.
"Every effort shall be made" and "jobs most nearly equivalent" set no standard a court could apply, and the sentence's opening words are garbled beyond reconstruction.
"To the extent practicable" is an undefined qualifier, and "advance product production at Carlstadt" is not defined anywhere in the instrument.

The absolute command that the arbitrator "shall issue his award before operations commence" is immediately qualified by the next sentence providing for what happens if he does not, so the mandate's force is uncertain.

It is unclear whether mediation on either party's written request is a condition precedent to arbitration ("prior to arbitration") or merely an optional attempt, since the parties only "agree to attempt".

"Any labor organization" is followed by a closed parenthetical list of nine named unions, leaving it uncertain whether an unlisted bargaining unit triggers the me-too right. The provisos turning on "productivity improvements or attrition" and benefits "diverted from an existing or subsequently negotiated wage and benefit package" are also undefined.

"Such agreements and ... documents, including but not limited to group contracts and trust agreements" is a general catch-all against two specifics, and "as are necessary to administer" leaves who judges necessity unstated.
The same open-ended "including but not limited to" formula against two named documents leaves the extent of The Times' execution obligation uncertain.

The carve-out is measured by "its obligation to make contributions required by the Contract for The Times deliverers", which is exactly the quantum the rest of the instrument leaves open, so the limit has no fixed content.

This disclaimer must be read against paragraph 2(a)'s pension-and-welfare direction and the Section 13-H.1 revision fixing 7.678% plus $3.67 per shift, and could be argued to cap obligations those provisions create.

The protected characteristics are an enumerated closed list (color, race, sex, religion, national origin) with no catch-all, so whether other grounds such as age or disability are covered turns on expressio unius.
"Group I employees not so scheduled" has no antecedent in the provision — nothing states what schedule is meant — so the class entitled to the new jury-pay measure is not identifiable from the text.

"A foreman or assistant foreman in each plant" leaves it open whether one supervisor per plant suffices or whether the Publisher may choose between the two ranks, and the opening "[w]henever the Publisher has one or more Plants" is a condition that is always satisfied.

This paragraph identifies the welfare-contribution letter as "Appendix C", but the letter as executed in the instrument is carried under an Appendix B designation, so the cross-reference does not match the attachment.
The Section 3-P letter is called "Appendix D" here, but the attached letters bear an Appendix B label, leaving the identification of the incorporated document uncertain.
The arbitrator-designation letter is called "Appendix E", yet the executed neutrals letter in the instrument is footed "Appendix B", so the cross-reference and the attachment disagree.

This blanket preservation of all prior side agreements "unless modified" sits uneasily with the Appendix B provision abolishing the November 22, 1983 West Side Direct Memorandum outright and with the September 9, 1988 side letter limiting that abolition.
"All dates in the Contract shall be updated to reflect this Memorandum" gives no rule for how any particular date is to be changed, so the instruction cannot be self-applied.

The priority rule works only if a "conflict" is identified, and it sits directly against the preceding sentence preserving all prior letter and side agreements in full force, so which text yields in a case of overlap rather than contradiction is open.

The promise to execute a consolidated "New York Times Agreement" raises the question, given paragraph 14's preservation clause, whether the unexecuted consolidated document or the surviving 1981-84 booklet and side letters governs.
Effectiveness on ratification (in 1988) has to be reconciled with paragraph 1's six-year term running from March 31, 1987 and the retroactive payment provisions in paragraph 2(a).

The whole undertaking is "[s]ubject to there being no increase in the number of floor hires as set forth in the Collective Bargaining Agreement", a condition whose baseline and consequence if breached are not stated.

"Shall continue to be served by" preserves an existing practice without describing it, and "delivery points designated by the Publisher" leaves the Publisher's discretion over the routemen's work unbounded.
The Times gets "the right to reorganize these routes" subject only to the number of routes not being reduced, a proviso that does not say whether route content, size or manning may be altered.

The September 9, 1988 West Side Directs side letter says the "abolition" affects nothing in the 1983 Memorandum other than the attrition portion, which cuts against reading this sentence as an outright abolition.

The cross-reference is to "Appendix B-1", but the honor-box side letter in the instrument is carried under the Appendix B footer with no B-1 designation, so the referenced document is not cleanly identified.
"The headsheet or other designated portion of each copy" leaves the returnable portion to later designation, and the exception for "unsold current copies on 'bulldog' routes" is not defined.

The preservation of "any existing physical pick-up of such copies" is hard to square with the immediately preceding sentence requiring that all returns be handled by mailing the headsheet to the Publisher.
"Maintain present Practices" identifies no practices and fixes no date at which they are measured, so the content of the obligation is entirely extrinsic.

The August 30, 1988 counsel letter enclosing the Spinelli memorandum purports to fix what these "present practices" are for the West Side Direct operation, which may narrow or contradict the letter's reference to "The Times direct operation" generally.

The letter changes only the frequency of "contributions to the Welfare Fund" without saying which contributions — the percentage contribution, the $3.67 per shift, or the casual per-shift amounts — are made weekly.
It must be read with the revised Section 13-H.1 (7.678% plus $3.67 per shift, and per-shift casual amounts), which fixes the amounts this timing letter assumes but does not identify.
"Made available" is not the same as paid or received, and it is not stated to whom or how availability is measured, leaving the moment of compliance open.

The definition fixes the relationship "at the time the grandparent dies", which does not resolve whether step- or in-law grandparents of a spouse qualify, the very inconsistency the letter was written to cure.

A letter that "shall not have retroactive effect" while purporting only to confirm the existing meaning of Section 3-P is in tension with paragraph 12, which describes it as The Times' interpretation of the existing contract.
The quoted replacement sentence is garbled and incomplete ("may elect to accumulate a ll ef hi ... leave days"), so the amendment's operative words cannot be read.
The neutrals are "identified" but not named, and the obligation is only to meet "to effectuate the designation process" — no process, criteria or fallback is stated.
An obligation to "negotiate the conditions" is an agreement to agree with no standard of performance, and "the normal daily order" of 2500 copies is not defined or measured over any stated period.
The commitment is only to "discuss and identify the present problems", which fixes no obligation capable of breach.

The assignment is triggered both by agreement on "satisfactory arrangements" that are "in operation" and by an outside date tied to "the revised Glen Burnie agreement", and it is not clear which controls if no revised agreement is ever made.
"Shall not involve The Times in increased costs" gives no baseline against which costs are compared and no measure of what counts as an increase.

The duty is only to "negotiate ... the arrangements" after grievances are "resolved satisfactorily" — both the trigger and the obligation are unmeasurable, and the no-increased-costs proviso has no baseline.

Item (b) inserts "an after tax deduction from wages of $3.67" into the contribution sentence with an unclosed quotation, so whether the $3.67 is an employer contribution or an employee wage deduction, and how it interacts with the 7.678% figure, cannot be read off the text.
The same $3.67 appears in paragraph 2(a) as an amount "contributed to the Welfare Fund" with a five-shift cap, and the two texts may state one obligation or two, and only one of them carries the cap.
"Regularly inserted in the Sunday or daily newspaper" is an undefined frequency test that determines whether the notice obligation applies at all.
"The promptest practicable notice" sets no ascertainable deadline, and what The Times must "demonstrate" about its own lack of sixty days' notice, and to whom, is unstated.
The exception swallows the sixty-day requirement just inserted by the preceding amendment, so the two sentences of the same amendment pull against each other.

"A uniform portion of each employee's wage increase" does not say who fixes the portion or over what group uniformity is measured, and whether the Union may exercise the diversion unilaterally is left open by "the Union may divert".
"Nominal administrative costs" is an undefined threshold that alone limits The Times' exposure under the diversion right.
"Fully cooperate ... in developing any such alternatives" is an undefined standard of effort, and "alternatives" is broader than the vacation-pay diversion the letter actually grants.

The guarantee is incomplete on its face — "it will guarantee all Saturday night Bulldog uding routes and relays" omits what is guaranteed (situations? work?) — so the promise cannot be read from the text.
This subparagraph adds to "gross wages" amounts that paragraph 4(a) defines by reference to the W-2 form alone, so the definition and its exception must be reconciled.

"The applicable bonus period" is used here without definition; paragraphs 2 and 3 supply calendar years and a January-March 1993 stub, and paragraph 6 sets a different thirty-day deadline for that stub period.

"$25.93 at the Union's option shall be added to the weekly wage scales or allocated in the manner set forth in Paragraph 7" does not say what happens if the Union exercises no option, and Paragraph 7 describes a separate termination right rather than an allocation manner.

Paragraph 7 lets the Union terminate the Earnings Bonus only "during the term of the Contract" on thirty days' notice, which is hard to square with this automatic cessation and allocation on March 31, 1993.

The string "apply $25.93 to the weekly wage scales or to any fringe benefit ... provided under the contract or negotiated by any other union and the Times in connection with the current extension negotiations or at any time through March 30, 1993" is syntactically ambiguous as to what the trailing time phrases modify.

"Any benefit provided to employees ... which is calculated on or determined by the employee's wage rate" is a broad catch-all whose reach — in particular whether employer contributions to jointly-trusteed funds are such a "benefit" — is not fixed.

The closing sentence of the same paragraph 8 says nothing "herein" requires Welfare or Pension Fund contributions calculated as if wages were increased by $25.93, which directly cuts back this general rule and leaves the boundary contested.

This sentence expressly includes "Times retirement or pension benefits" in the $25.93 uplift, while the last sentence of paragraph 8 excludes contributions to the NMDU-Publishers' Pension Fund calculated on that uplift, and the two are difficult to harmonise.

"Applied so as to eliminate any duplication of the Earnings benefit or wage rate" is opaque — it names no benefit that would be duplicated and gives no rule for which of two overlapping calculations yields.

"Nothing herein" may reach only paragraph 8 or the whole Earnings Bonus letter, and the carve-out addresses contributions on Earnings Bonus payments and on the $25.93 uplift without saying what the contribution base otherwise is.

It excludes Welfare and Pension Fund contributions from the very uplift that the opening sentences of paragraph 8 (including the express reference to "Times retirement or pension benefits") require for wage-rate-based benefits.
The provision states a bare number without saying what it counts, depending entirely on the first sentence of a Paragraph 3 in the 1981-84 contract book that is not reproduced here.

This side letter preserves everything in the November 22, 1983 Memorandum except the attrition portion, whereas the Appendix B home-delivery text says that Memorandum "shall be abolished" and gives The Times the right to reorganize the routes.
